57.title: Hillel on one foot
57.hook: asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel says: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, the rest is commentary, go and learn (Talmud, Shabbat 31a)
57.howItsDone: Jews study Hillel's answer in the Talmud, Shabbat 31a, and it is often taught to children as a first summary of Jewish ethics, always together with its last words: go and learn.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was wu wei: the swimmer went down with the swirl and came up singing. Your line was go with the water. Today starts a new week: Jewish wisdom tales.

Somebody asks you to explain your whole job, your whole faith, your whole life's philosophy, in one sentence. Go. Right now. It's a slightly rude question, and a slightly brilliant one. Two thousand years ago, in Jerusalem, a man walked up to two of the greatest rabbis of his day with a version of it. The Talmud tells the story. He said: teach me the entire Torah, all of it, while I stand on one foot. The first rabbi, Shammai, chased him away. The second was Hillel.
screen: `EXPLAIN IT IN ONE SENTENCE.` → `TEACH ME ON ONE FOOT.` → `SHAMMAI, THEN HILLEL.`

segments.voice: It's in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page thirty-one. A man who isn't Jewish asks Shammai to teach him the whole Torah on one foot. Shammai, famously strict, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick he's holding. So he tries Hillel. Hillel doesn't send him away. He answers in Aramaic, short enough to say standing on one foot. What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Three things happen in that answer. First, the center. The Talmud doesn't name a verse here, but many readers hear behind it the commandment in Leviticus, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society wording, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," put in its most practical form: don't do to others what you hate. You met a version of this on day fifteen of this path, the golden rule, and it lives in many traditions. Second, the rest is commentary: not unimportant, but built around that center. Third, the part people forget: now go and learn. Hillel doesn't say the one line is enough. He gives the summary, then sends the man to study. The whole teaching fits on one foot. Living it takes two feet and the rest of your life. Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says, often disagreed, and their schools argued for generations. Jewish tradition kept both sides of their arguments, and remembers Hillel especially for his patience.
screen: `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` · `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` · `THE ONE LINE ISN'T THE END.` · then, large: `NOW GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand on one foot; if standing isn't right for you, sit tall and lift one hand instead. Find your balance and say quietly: what is hateful to me, I won't do to my neighbor, and wobble if you wobble. Then put your foot down, breathe, and think of one thing you'd hate someone to do to you that you might be tempted to do to someone else.
Zil g'mor, Aramaic for go, learn. Hillel's last words to the man standing on one foot, after summing up the whole Torah in a single line.
Your line: now go and learn. The summary is short, and the learning is long. Fifty-seven days, and counting.

58.title: Honi and the carob tree
58.hook: an old man plants a tree that won't fruit for seventy years, for his grandchildren (Talmud, Taanit 23a)
58.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Honi in the Talmud, Taanit 23a, and it is a familiar retelling around Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was zil g'mor: Hillel taught the whole Torah on one foot, then said go and learn. Your line was now go and learn.

Somebody planted the tree whose shade you last sat in. Somebody laid out the park, stocked the library, worked out the recipe a family still makes, knowing they would never meet the people who'd use it. The Talmud has a story about this, and about a man named Honi. Tradition remembers him as a holy man in the land of Israel, Honi the Circle-Drawer, because once, in a drought, he drew a circle on the ground and would not step out of it until it rained. One day Honi is walking along a road, and he sees an old man planting a tree.
screen: `SOMEONE STARTED IT FOR YOU.` → `HONI THE CIRCLE-DRAWER.` → `AN OLD MAN PLANTING A TREE.`

segments.voice: It begins with a verse that bothered Honi, from a psalm about the return from exile. In the King James words: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream." Seventy years in exile, like a dream. Can a person really sleep seventy years? So Honi is on the road, turning that over, when he sees the old man planting a carob tree. How long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the man. Are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? And the old man says, more or less: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it. My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children. Then Honi sits down to eat, and falls asleep. Rocks grow up around him, hiding him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree. Are you the one who planted it? No, says the man. I'm his grandson. The story ends sadly: back home, nobody believes he's Honi, and he feels so alone that he no longer wants to live. The rabbis draw a saying from it: companionship or death. But the heart of the first part is the old man, planting. He does the work, and the fruit belongs to someone he'll never meet. He got here under trees he didn't plant, and he knows it.

segments.voice: Look around and find one thing near you that someone made or planted before you, a tree outside, a building, a word you use, and thank them silently, whoever they were. Then think of one small thing you could start for someone after you: a seed in a pot, a note for your kids, money set aside, a skill you teach.

59.title: Why weren't you Zusya?
59.hook: Rabbi Zusya fears heaven won't ask why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya (Hasidic tale)
59.howItsDone: Zusya's question is retold in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Hasidic tales like it are still passed on aloud in Hasidic communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was haruv: an old man planted a carob tree for grandchildren he'd never meet. Your line was for the ones after.

Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better than you. A better cook. A better parent. Someone your age who's already written the book, run the marathon, started the company. It's easy to feel like you're failing at being them. The Hasidic tales of Eastern Europe tell of a rabbi named Zusya, known for being poor, humble and full of joy. Near the end of his life, his students find him weeping, afraid. They're amazed. What could a man like Zusya possibly fear?
screen: `SOMEONE DOING YOUR LIFE BETTER.` → `RABBI ZUSYA, WEEPING.` → `WHAT COULD HE FEAR?`

segments.voice: Rabbi, the students say, why are you afraid? You've been as faithful as Moses. As kind as Abraham. And Zusya answers: when I come before the heavenly court, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? I'd have an answer for that: I wasn't given what Moses was given. They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham? I wasn't Abraham. They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say then? The story comes from the Hasidim, a movement of joyful, mystical renewal among the Jews of Eastern Europe. Their stories were told aloud before anyone wrote them down, and later collectors, Martin Buber among them, carried this one into print. Notice what Zusya refuses to do. Measure yourself against the greatest person you can imagine, and anyone comes up short. Zusya says that isn't the test. Nobody will ask you to be Moses. The question is harder and kinder at once: did you become the person only you could be? Did you use what you were actually given, your hands, your voice, your odd mix of gifts and wounds? Harder, because you can't hide behind I'm not Moses. Kinder, because nobody is asking you to be anyone else. Zusya couldn't answer for Moses. He could only answer for Zusya.
screen: `WHY WEREN'T YOU MOSES?` · `A TALE FROM THE HASIDIM.` · `MEASURED AGAINST SOMEONE ELSE.` · `HARDER, AND KINDER.` · then, large: `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?`

segments.voice: Let go of the person you've been comparing yourself to; let them walk off. Then ask quietly: what do I have that's mine? A way of making people laugh, a particular kindness, something you notice that others don't: hold one, and picture one small way to use it, the way only you would.
Zusya. A Hasidic rabbi who feared one question: not why weren't you someone greater, but why weren't you yourself.
Your line: be zusya. The only question is the one with your own name in it. That's day fifty-nine.

60.title: Two pockets
60.hook: Rabbi Simcha Bunim keeps two notes: "for my sake the world was created" and "I am dust and ashes" (Hasidic tale, drawing on Sanhedrin 37a and Genesis 18:27)
60.howItsDone: Simcha Bunim's two pockets are taught in Jewish schools and sermons, and some people do carry the two notes; the lines come from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Zusya, who feared one question: why weren't you Zusya? Your line was be zusya.

Two slips of paper. That's all today needs. On a bad day a person can feel like nothing: small, useless, invisible. On another day, the same person can feel like the center of the universe, the smartest one in the room, owed something by everyone. It's possible to swing between the two in a single afternoon, and to reach for the wrong feeling at the wrong moment. There's a Hasidic teaching for exactly this, told of Rabbi Simcha Bunim, a Hasidic master in Poland. Every person, he said, should carry two pockets, each with a slip of paper inside.
screen: `SOME DAYS, NOTHING.` → `SOME DAYS, THE CENTER.` → `CARRY TWO POCKETS.`

segments.voice: In one pocket, a note: for my sake the world was created. In the other: I am dust and ashes. The teaching is simply this: know which one to reach for. Both lines come from much older sources. The first is from the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin. It asks why the Bible tells of one single human being created at the beginning, and answers, in part: to teach that a single life counts as a whole world. So, it says, each person should say: for my sake the world was created. The second is from Genesis. Abraham is standing before God, bargaining for the city of Sodom, pleading for any good people who might live there. In the King James words he says he has dared to speak to the Lord, "which am but dust and ashes." Notice: Abraham says it while he is boldly arguing with God. Humility and courage in the same breath. So when do you reach for which? When you feel worthless, crushed, sure your life doesn't matter: the first pocket. The world was made for you, too. Your life counts as a whole world. And when you feel proud, sure you're above someone, about to be cruel because you can: the second. Dust and ashes. The trick isn't choosing one note forever. It's carrying both, and knowing which the moment needs. Neither is the whole truth alone. Together, they're a person.

segments.voice: If you have paper, tear two small slips: on one write, for my sake the world was created, on the other, I am dust and ashes, and put one in each pocket. If you don't have paper, hold one hand, then the other. Then ask: which pocket does today need?
Two pockets. One note says the world was made for you; the other says you are dust and ashes. Reach for the one the moment needs.
Your line: reach for the right pocket. Feeling small, the world; feeling too big, the dust. Sixty days now.

61.title: The boy with the whistle
61.hook: an unlettered boy whistles in the synagogue on Yom Kippur, and the Baal Shem Tov says his whistle opened the gates (Hasidic tale)
61.howItsDone: Jews observe Yom Kippur with a full day of fasting and prayer that ends with Neilah, the closing service, and the shofar's blast; the tale of the whistling boy is told in Hasidic communities and sermons around the holy day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two pockets: the world was made for you, and you are dust and ashes. Your line was reach for the right pocket.

Have you ever been somewhere sacred, a wedding, a funeral, a service, and felt like you didn't know the words? Everyone else is singing along, standing and sitting at the right times, and you're mouthing something, hoping nobody notices. This story is for anyone who's felt that. It's a Hasidic tale from Eastern Europe, told about the Baal Shem Tov, whom Hasidic tradition remembers as its founder. It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. The synagogue is packed. People have fasted and prayed since the night before. And at the back stands a village boy who can't read a word of the prayer book.
screen: `NOT KNOWING THE WORDS.` → `YOM KIPPUR, THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` → `A BOY WHO CAN'T READ.`

segments.voice: The boy's father has brought him, worried. The boy is simple, the story says, a shepherd boy with a little whistle he plays for the sheep. His father made him promise to keep it in his pocket. All day the boy stands there, watching everyone pray words he can't follow. He wants to join in. He has nothing to join with. It's growing late. The final prayer of the day has begun, the one the tradition calls Neilah, the closing, when the gates of heaven are pictured swinging shut. And the boy can't hold it in anymore. He pulls out his whistle and blows one loud, shrill note, right in the middle of the closing prayer. The whole room turns. People are furious. His father is mortified. The Baal Shem Tov stops, then finishes the prayer, and afterward, the story says, he tells them: the gates were closed. All our prayers, all our learned words, were stuck. And that boy's whistle, from a whole heart, broke through, and carried our prayers up with it. The story has been told in many versions. Hasidic tales like this one honor simple, heartfelt devotion alongside learning. Jewish tradition treasures study deeply; this tale doesn't reject it. It says the heart can get through too, even when the words won't come. The whistle got through because it was all the boy had, and he gave all of it.

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're grateful for today, and instead of finding perfect words, give thanks however it comes out: hum a note, tap your hand on your knee, say thanks out loud, badly. If you pray, you can say it in your own words, however rough. It doesn't need to be beautiful; it needs to be yours, and whole.
Neilah, the closing prayer of Yom Kippur. A boy who couldn't read blew his whistle during it, and the Baal Shem Tov said it opened the gates.
Your line: the whistle got through. One shrill note, from a whole heart. Day sixty-one, done.

62.title: The treasure under the bridge
62.hook: Isaac of Kraków travels to Prague for a dreamed treasure and learns it's under his own stove (Hasidic tale)
62.howItsDone: The tale of Isaac of Kraków is told in Hasidic teaching about finding what's sacred close to home, and the old synagogue in Kraków's Kazimierz district that bears the name of Isaac son of Jacob is often linked to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Neilah, the closing prayer of Yom Kippur, when a boy's whistle broke through. Your line was the whistle got through.

Somewhere out there is the thing that will fix everything. The better city. The better job. The retreat in the mountains. The person who finally gets you. A lot of life goes into planning the trip to go and get it. There's a Hasidic tale about a man who actually made that trip: Isaac, the son of Yekel, a poor, devout man in Kraków, in Poland. Night after night, he dreams the same dream: go to Prague, and under the bridge that leads to the king's castle, you'll find a treasure. The third time he has the dream, he packs a bag.
screen: `THE THING THAT WILL FIX EVERYTHING.` → `ISAAC OF KRAKÓW.` → `GO TO PRAGUE.`

segments.voice: It's a long walk from Kraków to Prague. When Isaac gets there, he finds the bridge, guarded by soldiers day and night, and he doesn't dare dig. So every day he comes back and circles it, until the captain of the guard notices and asks, kindly enough, what he's looking for. Isaac, having nothing to lose, tells him about the dream. And the captain laughs. You walked all this way because of a dream? If I believed in dreams, I'd have gone to Kraków long ago! I keep dreaming there's a treasure under the stove of some Jew called Isaac, son of Yekel. Imagine walking all that way, where half the men are called Isaac and the other half Yekel! Isaac thanks him, walks all the way home, digs under his own stove, and finds the treasure. Tradition says he used it to build a synagogue, and in Kraków there is still one known by his name. Martin Buber's collection records Rabbi Simcha Bunim, the teacher of the two pockets, telling this story to young men who came to him for the first time. He'd add something like: there's something you can't find anywhere in the world, not even with a great teacher, but there is a place where you can find it. The same story turns up in other homes too: in the Thousand and One Nights and in Rumi, it's a man of Baghdad who dreams of Cairo. But notice: Isaac still had to make the journey. The trip didn't hold the treasure. It showed him where it had been all along.

Look for something good you've stopped seeing: a person, a window with light, a chair that holds you, a cup you love, a plant still alive despite you. Stop there, and dig a little.

63.title: Where does God live?
63.hook: the Kotzker Rebbe answers his students: wherever people let God in (Hasidic tale)
63.tomorrow: the north wind and the sun
63.howItsDone: The Kotzker's saying is quoted in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Jewish homes traditionally have a mezuzah on the doorposts, which some people touch on the way in and out as a reminder of God's presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was otzar, treasure: Isaac walked to Prague to learn his was under his own stove. Your line was it was under the stove.

Kids ask the best questions. Where was I before I was born? Why is the sky that color? And, sooner or later: if God is real, where does God live? Adults tend to answer fast, and a little embarrassed: everywhere, sweetie. Menachem Mendel of Kotzk, known as the Kotzker Rebbe, wasn't satisfied with the fast answer. He was a Hasidic master in Poland, remembered as fierce, brilliant and allergic to anything fake. One day, the tale goes, he turns to a room of learned visitors and asks them that exact question: where does God live?
screen: `KIDS ASK THE BEST QUESTIONS.` → `THE KOTZKER REBBE.` → `WHERE DOES GOD LIVE?`

segments.voice: The visitors laugh. What a question, Rebbe! Everyone knows the answer. The prophet Isaiah says it. In his vision, the seraphim call out, in the King James words: "the whole earth is full of his glory." God is everywhere. And the Kotzker shakes his head. No, he says. God lives wherever people let God in. One small sentence, and the whole picture changes. The visitors' answer is true in their tradition: God fills the world. But the rebbe is asking something else. Not where God is in theory, but where God is actually at home: where a presence is welcomed, noticed, given room. A house can be full of air and still feel shut. The Hebrew tradition has a word for God's indwelling presence, Shekhinah, from a root that means to dwell, to live somewhere. The Kotzker's point is that the dwelling isn't only up to God. It's also a door that people open, or keep closed. For listeners who don't use the word God, the story still speaks: whatever you call what's sacred, awe, love, presence, it tends to live where it's let in. Now look back at this week. zil g'mor. haruv. Zusya's question. Two pockets. The whistle. The treasure under the stove. And now, where does God live. Seven tales from Jewish tradition, and nearly every one turns on something small and close: one line, one tree, one self, one note, one whistle, one stove, one open door.

If you pray, let God in, in your own way; if you don't, let in whatever is sacred to you: stillness, gratitude, the day itself.
Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence. The Kotzker Rebbe's answer to where God lives: wherever people let God in.
Your line: let it in. The door is yours to open. That closes the Jewish wisdom week, day sixty-three.
